ai.definition: Precision oncology is an approach that uses molecular profiling to identify the specific genetic alterations driving a patient's cancer, enabling targeted therapies tailored to the individual patient.
ai.howItWorks: Liquid biopsies involve collecting blood samples from patients, which are then analyzed using advanced sequencing technologies. These techniques can detect circulating tumor cells and fragments of DNA (ctDNA) that provide information about the genomic landscape of the cancer. This data is used to tailor treatment plans for each patient.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional biopsy methods often require invasive procedures and may not capture the full genetic profile of a patient's cancer. Liquid biopsies offer a non-invasive alternative, providing real-time monitoring of disease progression and response to therapy without the need for repeated invasive procedures.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and validating liquid biopsy assays, which include sample collection devices, extraction kits, and sequencing platforms. These components are typically produced in specialized laboratories with stringent quality control measures.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the assay to target specific genetic markers, optimizing the extraction of ctDNA from blood samples, and integrating this with high-throughput sequencing technologies. Validation studies are conducted to ensure accuracy and reliability before clinical use.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of advanced sequencing technologies, the cost of reagents for sample preparation and sequencing, and the need for specialized laboratory equipment. Additionally, the complexity of analyzing large volumes of genomic data adds to the overall expense.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for precision oncology is positive as it addresses unmet needs in cancer diagnosis and treatment. However, regulatory approval processes can be lengthy and costly, which may delay market entry.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by country but generally require rigorous clinical trials to demonstrate safety and efficacy before approval. Key regulatory bodies include the FDA (U.S.) and EMA (Europe).
ai.risks: Risks include the potential for false positives or negatives, the need for accurate sample handling and analysis, and the high costs associated with developing and validating these technologies.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable but can be significant once established. High margins are possible due to the specialized nature of the technology and the willingness of healthcare providers to invest in precision oncology solutions.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may focus on improving the sensitivity and specificity of liquid biopsies, integrating machine learning algorithms for better predictive analytics, and expanding coverage to include a wider range of cancers and genetic markers.

glossary.def: A method for detecting cancer by analyzing circulating tumor cells or DNA in a blood sample, providing non-invasive monitoring of disease.
Cells that break away from the primary tumor and enter the bloodstream, potentially contributing to metastasis.
Fragments of DNA released by dying cancer cells into the bloodstream, which can be sequenced to identify genetic mutations associated with cancer.

subsystems.name: Tumour profiling pipeline
subsystems.role: finds the specific mutations that make one person's cancer vulnerable.

subsystems.name: Gene-editing toolkit
subsystems.role: cuts or rewrites DNA at a chosen site in a cell.
parts: Cas9 nuclease, base editor or prime editor protein

subsystems.name: Delivery system
subsystems.role: gets the editing machinery into the right cells and nowhere else.

subsystems.name: Engineered cell therapy
subsystems.role: turns the patient's own immune cells into cancer killers.
parts: chimeric antigen receptor or T-cell receptor construct

subsystems.name: Targeted drugs
subsystems.role: block the protein a mutation drives, or deliver a toxin to cells carrying a marker.

subsystems.name: Clinical decision and monitoring layer
subsystems.role: decides which therapy fits and tracks whether it is working.

buildSteps.title: Sample the tumour
buildSteps.detail: A needle biopsy of a few millimetres, or a blood draw of a few millilitres for circulating tumour DNA when a biopsy is risky.

buildSteps.title: Sequence and interpret
buildSteps.detail: Hundreds of cancer genes, or the whole exome, are read and compared with the patient's normal DNA to separate driver mutations from harmless variation.

buildSteps.title: Choose the target and the edit
buildSteps.detail: The team picks either a mutated protein to drug, or an immune gene to edit out — for example a checkpoint gene that would otherwise switch the engineered cell off.

buildSteps.title: Design and build the payload
buildSteps.detail: Guide RNA sequences are chosen by software, the editing protein is synthesised as mRNA, and off-target sites are predicted and then measured in donor cells.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture the therapy
buildSteps.detail: For a cell product, T cells are collected by apheresis, edited outside the body by electroporation, grown to billions of cells over roughly one to two weeks, then frozen.

buildSteps.title: Run quality control
buildSteps.detail: Each batch is checked for sterility, correct edit, unwanted edits, and the ability to actually kill target cells before it is released.

buildSteps.title: Treat the patient
buildSteps.detail: Short chemotherapy clears space in the immune system, then the edited cells are infused — or, for an in-body approach, the editing particles are dosed directly.

buildSteps.title: Monitor response and toxicity
buildSteps.detail: Falling circulating tumour DNA and shrinking scans mean it is working; cytokine release and immune attack on normal tissue are watched for closely.

buildSteps.title: Re-profile on relapse
buildSteps.detail: Tumours evolve, so a new sample is sequenced and the next therapy chosen against the resistance mutation that appeared.

prerequisites.why: profiling a tumour costs a fraction of what it did a decade ago and is routine in many hospitals.
first used to edit human cells in 2012; base and prime editors now allow single-letter changes without a double-strand break. Clinical use is still early.

prerequisites.tech: Safe, targeted delivery in the body
prerequisites.why: lipid nanoparticles reach the liver well but other organs poorly, which limits which cancers can be edited directly rather than in a lab dish.
patient-specific cell therapies need cleanroom time and specialist staff that most hospitals do not have.

prerequisites.tech: Knowledge of which mutations are actionable
prerequisites.why: only a minority of mutations found have a drug or edit that changes the outcome; the rest are unresolved.
decades of follow-up are needed to rule out edits landing in the wrong place and causing a new cancer.

pathway.milestone: sequencing panels and biomarker-matched drugs are standard care in major cancer centres; engineered cell therapies are approved for some blood cancers and melanoma
pathway.unlocks: real, if narrow, survival gains for patients whose tumour carries the right marker.

pathway.milestone: CRISPR-edited cell therapies move from small trials to approved products
pathway.unlocks: treatments for patients who relapse after current cell therapies, because edited cells resist exhaustion.

pathway.milestone: editing delivered directly in the body by lipid nanoparticles
pathway.unlocks: avoids the cost and delay of extracting, editing and re-infusing a patient's own cells.

pathway.milestone: off-the-shelf donor cells with multiple edits to evade rejection
pathway.unlocks: treatment that can start within days rather than weeks, and at far lower cost.

pathway.milestone: editing used alongside standard therapy and against resistance mutations
pathway.unlocks: durable remissions rather than a few months of extra disease control.
